analysis.one_liner: Bans unregulated "soft money" donations to national political parties and requires unions to refund non-members' fees spent on politics.
analysis.headline: A majority of the Senate supported it—votes to end debate came out 52-48 and 53-47—but that fell short of the 60 needed, and the bill died without a final vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban national party committees from raising or spending "soft money"—the large donations from corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals that avoid federal contribution limits and disclosure rules. It would require party spending on federal elections to come from regulated funds, stop parties from funneling money to tax-exempt groups, and require labor unions to reduce non-members' fees by the share spent on political activity. It also raised some individual contribution limits as a trade-off.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, whose elections would no longer be financed in part by unlimited, largely undisclosed soft money; and non-union employees covered by union contracts, who could opt out of the portion of their fees that goes to politics.

how_it_helps.text: Bars national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending money outside the limits and reporting rules of federal election law, closing the soft-money channel.

Requires state and local party committees to pay for federal election activity—voter registration drives, get-out-the-vote work, and ads naming federal candidates—from funds that follow federal limits and disclosure rules.
Prohibits party committees from soliciting funds for or donating to tax-exempt organizations, a common route for money to avoid disclosure.
Extends the ban to federal candidates and incumbents and entities they control, so campaigns cannot raise or direct unregulated money.
Requires national and state party committees to report all receipts and disbursements, including itemized reporting of anyone giving more than $200.

Writes the Supreme Court's Beck decision into law: employees who are not union members but pay fees under a union contract can object once a year and have their payments reduced by the share spent on politics unrelated to collective bargaining.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees lose unlimited soft money; large donors, corporations, and unions lose an unregulated way to fund elections and must accept disclosure; unions lose some fee income from non-members when the political share is refunded.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the individual aggregate contribution limit from $25,000 to $30,000 and creates a new $10,000 annual limit for state party committees—giving the biggest donors somewhat more regulated room even as it closes soft money.

The bill restricts party and candidate money but does not limit advertising by outside groups that praise or attack a candidate without explicitly urging a vote, so money could shift to unregulated outside organizations.
The Beck provision, a long-standing Republican priority, cuts into unions' ability to use non-member fee income for politics, which unions argued was an unfair one-sided burden in the name of reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change—banning party soft money and extending disclosure—would have removed the least accountable major funding stream in federal elections, a real benefit to ordinary voters. The offsetting increase in individual limits was modest by comparison. The main weakness was design: by touching parties and candidates but not outside issue-advocacy groups, it left open an escape hatch that money would likely have used.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate debated the bill in October 1999, but two votes to end debate on amendments each fell short of the 60 needed—52-48 and 53-47—so the bill never reached a final vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain (R-AZ) introduced the bill for himself and Senator Russell Feingold on September 16, 1999, and it was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee.
On October 8 the committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Senate calendar, ready for floor debate.
The Senate debated the bill from October 13 to October 19, 1999, with amendments by Democratic Senators Daschle and Reid pending.
On October 19, cloture on the Daschle amendment failed 52-48—only 52 of the 60 votes needed to end debate—so the amendment could not come to a vote.
Minutes later, cloture on the Reid amendment also failed 53-47.

Every Democrat present (45 of 45) voted to end debate both times, while only 7 and then 8 of 55 Republicans did; with the 60-vote threshold unmet, no further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The national party committees of both parties, which continued raising unlimited soft money through the 2000 elections, and the large donors and corporations that gave it, were better off because the bill died.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the campaign finance reform bill and led its Senate floor push.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Joined McCain as co-lead of the bill, which was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Feingold'.

for.name: 45 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously to end debate on the Daschle and Reid amendments, both times.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Offered an amendment during floor debate; a cloture motion on it was presented and failed 52-48.

against.name: 48 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on ending debate on the Daschle amendment (48 of 55) and the Reid amendment (47 of 55), dooming both cloture votes.

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Opposed campaign finance reform and, as majority leader, controlled which amendments and votes reached the floor during the October 1999 debate.

sides.party_line_note: The split was nearly unanimous by party: all 45 Democrats voted to end debate both times, while only 7 and 8 of 55 Republicans did, leaving the 52-48 and 53-47 tallies short of the 60 needed.

industries.note: The bill cut off their unlimited soft-money fundraising and forced federal election spending into disclosed, regulated funds. Both parties had built fundraising operations on that money, and its loss would have reduced a channel of influence unavailable to ordinary donors.

industries.industry: Large donors, corporations, and unions seeking political influence
industries.note: The biggest givers could no longer route unlimited money through party committees. The cost of their political access was borne by voters who cannot write six-figure checks.
The Beck provision requires unions to refund non-members the portion of fees spent on politics unrelated to collective bargaining, reducing the money available for union political activity.
The bill bars party committees from soliciting or donating funds to 501(c) tax-exempt groups, closing a route money used to avoid disclosure.
